title: Scientists Map Global Underground Fungal Networks Stretching 110 Quadrillion km, Near a Billion Sun Trips
body:
Scientists have unveiled the staggering scale of the planet’s underground fungal highways, estimating that arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi weave together roughly 110 quadrillion kilometres of living thread in the upper 15 centimetres of soil worldwide. That length is enough to stretch from Earth to the Sun almost a billion times, a figure that underscores the hidden but vital role these microscopic networks play in ecosystems, agriculture and climate regulation.

The international consortium behind the discovery, coordinated by the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), combined high‑resolution DNA sequencing, remote sensing of soil carbon and advanced modelling to chart the distribution of AM fungi across grasslands, forests, tundra and croplands. Their calculations suggest that about 40 percent of the total fungal thread resides beneath grassland soils, where the organisms form symbiotic relationships with the roots of grasses and herbaceous plants. In a single teaspoon of healthy soil, researchers can find up to ten metres of these delicate filaments, a density that multiplies into a planetary web of unimaginable length when extrapolated to the Earth’s surface.

Beyond the sheer magnitude, the findings highlight the ecological importance of AM fungi. These organisms extend the effective reach of plant roots, allowing trees and crops to access water and nutrients—particularly phosphorus and nitrogen—far beyond the immediate rhizosphere. In drought‑prone regions, the fungal network can act as a hydraulic conduit, redistributing moisture and buffering plants against stress. Moreover, the mycorrhizal threads sequester carbon within the soil matrix, contributing to long‑term storage of atmospheric CO₂ and thereby influencing global climate dynamics.

The study arrives at a critical moment for soil health initiatives worldwide. Intensive farming practices, heavy pesticide use and widespread soil disturbance have been shown to degrade mycorrhizal communities, reducing their capacity to support plant growth and carbon capture. By quantifying the sheer extent of these networks, the research provides a concrete metric for policymakers and land managers to gauge the impact of agricultural intensification and to justify investments in regenerative practices such as reduced tillage, cover cropping and organic amendments. Restoring and preserving AM fungal diversity could become a cornerstone of strategies aimed at feeding a growing population while mitigating greenhouse‑gas emissions.

Critics caution that the model’s reliance on indirect measurements introduces uncertainties, especially in regions with limited soil sampling. Nevertheless, the consensus among mycologists and ecologists is that the estimate, even if revised downward, will remain orders of magnitude larger than previous assumptions. The work also opens new avenues for interdisciplinary collaboration, linking microbiology, remote sensing, and climate science to monitor the health of the planet’s “hidden half.”

Looking ahead, the SPUN team plans to refine their map by incorporating real‑time monitoring sensors and expanding sampling to under‑represented biomes such as tropical rainforests and high‑altitude grasslands. As the scientific community deepens its understanding of these subterranean highways, the hope is that the data will translate into tangible actions—protecting soil biodiversity, enhancing food security and strengthening nature‑based climate solutions. In a world increasingly focused on visible megaprojects, the revelation that a microscopic network stretches across the globe, out‑lasting the distance to the Sun, serves as a humbling reminder of the profound influence of the unseen foundations of life.
